title: Psychiatrist surprised by Firman's behaviour
subtitle: Aron Firman's erratic and bizarre behaviour before he was Tasered by an OPP officer surprised his psychiatrist, an Coroner's inquest heard Friday.
article: Aron Firman's erratic and bizarre behaviour before he was Tasered by an OPP officer surprised his psychiatrist, an Coroner's inquest heard Friday.
"He never even came close to behaving in this manner," Dr. Michel Pigeon testified. "It's as if you were describing someone else. I can't make heads nor tails of this behaviour."
Dr. Pigeon, a psychiatrist with the Waypoint Centre for Mental Health, described Firman as "reasonable in his thought process" even though he had been suffering from schizophrenia.
"You could sit and have a nice talk with him, Pigeon told a five-person jury. "He understood the situation he was in."
But Firman was described as being "animalistic" on June 24 2010, the day he died after being Tasered at Collingwood's Blue Mountain Residence group home, where he lived.

Firman stormed one OPP officer and knocked down another before he was Tasered, the inquest heard earlier. The chief pathologist of Ontario determined Firman died of cardiac arrhythmia precipitated by the electric shocks from the Taser.
Firman was taking injections of an anti-psychotic drug to control schizophrenic symptoms in the week's leading up to the incident, the inquest heard.
But Taser International's lawyer David Neave pointed out the doses were far below what Pigeon had prescribed.
Firman was only injected with one-third of the dose he should have received between March 25 and June 16, Dr. Pigeon agreed while under cross-examination.
"He should have received 1,750 milligrams instead of 600," Neave said. "That would have provided him with a reservoir or a reserve that Mr. Firman would have needed during that period of time?"
"Correct," Dr. Pigeon replied.
Part of the problem was Firman did not receive any injections while he was in jail for three weeks in late May an early June, the inquest heard.
Firman's heavy dependence on marijuana would likely have exacerbated his psychotic symptoms as well, Dr. Pigeon testified.
Chronic marijuana use will dilute the effects of the anti-psychotic drug and can induce or mimic schizophrenic symptoms such as auditory hallucinations, Dr. Pigeon said.
Firman would kick the habit after a one-month stay in drug rehab only to smoke marijuana again the day he was released, the inquest heard.

"He said the first time he smoked marijuana it was like heaven. I think he was just trying to get back to that feeling," Dr. Pigeon testified. "Any person with psychosis who smokes marijuana, it will only get worse after a few days."

Firman's death is the first in Canada that a pathologist has attributed directly to the use of a Taser. In 2009, Amnesty International, the only organization to have compiled data on the issue, reported 334 fatalities following Taser jolts since 2001.
In 2010, the B.C. Supreme Court upheld findings of an inquiry into the death of Robert Dziekanski that the stun guns can kill.
Meanwhile, Taser International's lawyer suggested the anti-psychotic drug Firman was taking may have contributed to his death because some patients on the drug are susceptible to heart problems.
While Firman had been cleared to take the drug through electro-cardiagrams in 2007, he was not tested for possible heart issues from 2008 until the time of his death in June 2010.
"We know he received the doses and we had electro-cardiograms done that never showed any abnormalities whatsoever," Dr. Pigeon said.
"But he had no rhythm checks from 2008 to 2010, correct?" Neave asked.
"That's correct," Dr. Pigeon replied.
The inquest continues in Midhurst June 3.
